title: Joseph Bourgogne at NMAH: surviving commercial slide set, West Point accession cluster, and 1862 catalogue bridge
research_question: Can the Smithsonian boxed Bourgogne slide set be connected beyond maker attribution to a historical institutional address and then reverse-matched to Joseph Bourgogne's 1862 commercial catalogue?

principal_upgrade.previous_state: surviving boxed commercial endpoint attributed probably to Joseph Bourgogne; catalogue-to-object transcription open
principal_upgrade.new_state: The set sits in Smithsonian accession 217544, an accession cluster independently documented by NMAH as scientific teaching apparatus transferred from the U.S. Military Academy at West Point to the Smithsonian in 1958. The Bourgogne set also carries historical catalog number M-09791, the same catalog-number namespace as the Beck microscope MG.M-09791 from the U.S. Military Academy. This creates a strong accession-level institutional provenance bridge, while the direct item-level accession card and slide-label inventory remain open.

grade.joseph_bourgogne_attribution: A++/S-candidate — NMAH says the inscription is probably Joseph Bourgogne; label morphology and full transcription are still required for maker-generation certainty
grade.west_point_provenance: A++/S-candidate — common accession 217544 is repeatedly identified by NMAH as a 1958 West Point / U.S. Military Academy transfer, but the Bourgogne object page itself currently lacks an explicit credit line
grade.beck_microscope_association: A++ clue — Bourgogne set catalog number M-09791 overlaps the Beck microscope ID MG.M-09791, itself explicitly from the U.S. Military Academy; direct accessory/co-storage relation requires accession/object-card confirmation

direct_nmah_object_record.description_fact: NMAH states that the BOURGOGNE inscription on each slide in the set is probably that of Joseph Bourgogne, the Paris microscopist whose mounts won awards at international exhibitions.

basis.nmah_statement: Owned by the Department of Physics and Chemistry at the United States Military Academy, West Point, and transferred to the Smithsonian in 1958.
The West Point rack and tuning forks under this accession were transferred to the Smithsonian from West Point in 1958.
NMAH states that this ca. 1890 Beck microscope came from the U.S. Military Academy.
Purchased for the U.S. Military Academy in 1829.

accession_217544_cluster.cluster_character: Accession 217544 contains a broad historical teaching-apparatus transfer from West Point, including microscopes, optical apparatus, acoustical apparatus, balances, prisms and other classroom instruments. Multiple NMAH records explicitly carry U.S. Military Academy credit lines.
accession_217544_cluster.historical_implication: The Bourgogne set is no longer best treated merely as an isolated museum survival. Its accession address strongly places it within a historical scientific-teaching apparatus collection assembled at West Point and transferred as a collection cluster in 1958.

catalog_number_bridge.reading: The shared M-09791/M-9791 historical catalog-number namespace is a high-value clue that the Bourgogne slide set and Beck microscope were once catalogued together or under a common microscope-object grouping. Current public metadata does not state whether the slides were accessories to, stored with, or merely administratively associated with that microscope.
catalog_number_bridge.guard: Do not convert catalog-number overlap into an accessory or purchase-date claim without the accession 217544 file, original catalog card, or other internal NMAH documentation.

revised_chain: Paris commercial preparation and graded catalogue -> surviving Bourgogne-labelled two-box set -> probable West Point teaching-collection address via accession 217544 -> Smithsonian transfer in 1958 -> modern NMAH object record

why_it_matters.trade_history: The surviving endpoint now has a plausible institutional-use context rather than only modern museum custody.
why_it_matters.collection_history: The same slide set can be addressed by maker inscription, box membership, West Point accession context, old microscope catalog number and Smithsonian object ID.
why_it_matters.comparison_with_cole: Cole preserves publication identity through a fixed numbered cabinet. Bourgogne potentially preserves commodity identity inside a later teaching-apparatus collection. The two cases therefore test different ways in which commercial glass objects survived institutional re-addressing.
